title: A Turn Everyone Can See
bigQuestion: How do lines, sounds and signs help everyone see whose turn it is?

story.title: One Whistle, Two Groups
story.kicker: One short sound tells half the class to wait and half to go.
paragraphs: It is field day. Coach Lee stands by a white chalk line. Half of Room 104 waits behind it. The other half sits on the grass and watches.
Coach Lee lifts a silver whistle. One short blast! The runners dash across the grass. The sitters stay still. They know the whistle was not for them.

After the race, the groups trade places. A boy named Marcus asks, "How did everybody know what to do?" Coach Lee taps the line with her shoe. "This line and that sound are the same for everyone," she says.
story.think: What sounds or signs tell you it is your turn at school?

lessons.title: Stone Starting Lines
lessons.mainIdea: At Olympia, runners started from a line of stone slabs set into the ground.
reading: Ancient Greek runners needed a fair start. At Olympia, builders set long stone slabs into the ground at each end of the race path.
The Greeks called this stone start the *balbis*. It had grooves cut into the top. The grooves showed each runner where to stand. The stones are still there today.

words.d: the stone starting line in an ancient Greek stadium

look.title: A Line Made of Stone
look.text: Picture a row of flat gray stones in the dirt. Two long grooves are cut across the top. Small holes mark spaces for posts. Each space is for one runner.
look.prompt: Why is a stone line harder to cheat on than a line drawn in dirt?

check.q: What did the Greeks call the stone starting line?
check.why: The stone starting line in a Greek stadium was the balbis.

check.q: What was cut into the top of the starting stones?
check.why: Grooves in the stones showed runners where to stand.

check.q: Can people still see the starting stones at Olympia?
check.why: The stone starting line at Olympia can still be seen today.

lessons.title: Judges at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: Judges at Olympia watched the start and punished runners who left too soon.
reading: The Olympic Games had judges. Their Greek name meant "judges of the Greeks." They wore purple robes. They came from Elis, the city that ran the games.
Leaving before the signal is called a *false start*. Greek judges punished runners who did it. The old Greek writer Herodotus tells about this rule.

words.d: a person chosen to watch a contest and decide what is fair
leaving the starting line before the signal

look.title: A Talk Before a Battle
look.text: Herodotus tells of two Greek leaders arguing. One says that at the games, those who start too soon are punished. The other answers that those who are left behind win no crown.
look.prompt: What does this story tell us about starting early at the Greek games?

check.q: What is a false start?
check.why: A false start means leaving the line before the signal.

check.q: What color robes did the Olympic judges wear?
check.why: The judges at Olympia wore purple robes.

check.q: Which old Greek writer tells about punishing early starters?
check.why: Herodotus tells the story in Book 8 of his Histories.

lessons.title: A Whistle From Birmingham
lessons.mainIdea: Joseph Hudson made loud whistles in Birmingham, England, in the late 1800s.
reading: Joseph Hudson was a toolmaker in Birmingham, England. In the late 1800s, his company made loud metal *whistles*. London police officers carried them.
Football referees began using whistles in the same years. A whistle is louder than a voice. Everyone on a big field hears the same sound at once. Hudson's company, Acme, still makes whistles.

words.d: a small tool that makes a loud, high sound when you blow into it
the official who is in charge of a game

look.title: Voice or Whistle?
look.text: Picture a big grass field. Twenty-two players are running. A crowd is cheering. The referee shouts, "Stop!" Then the referee blows a whistle instead.
look.prompt: Which signal will reach the far side of the field? Why?

check.q: In which city did Joseph Hudson make whistles?
check.why: Joseph Hudson made whistles in Birmingham, England.

check.q: Who carried Hudson's whistles besides referees?
check.why: London police officers carried Hudson's whistles.

check.q: Why is a whistle helpful on a big field?
choices: It is quieter than a voice.
Only one player can hear it.
Everyone hears the same sound at once.
check.why: A whistle is louder than a voice, so the whole field hears it together.

lessons.title: The Referee Walks On
lessons.mainIdea: In 1891, the soccer referee moved onto the field with the power to decide.
reading: In early soccer, each team brought its own *umpire*. The two umpires stood on the field. A referee waited on the side. He decided only when the umpires did not agree.
In 1891, the rules changed. The referee walked onto the field. Now one person made the calls for both teams. The umpires moved to the sidelines and became linesmen.

words.d: an official who watches play and makes calls

look.title: Two Umpires or One Referee?
look.text: Picture two umpires. Each one was picked by a different team. A ball rolls near the line. One umpire says it was out. The other says it was in. Now picture one referee who decides for both teams.
look.prompt: Which way seems fairer to both teams? Why?

check.q: In early soccer, who brought the umpires?
check.why: Each team brought its own umpire in early soccer.

check.q: When did the referee move onto the soccer field?
check.why: The 1891 rule change put the referee on the field.

check.q: What did the old umpires become?
check.why: The umpires moved to the sidelines and became linesmen.

lessons.title: Yellow and Red Cards
lessons.mainIdea: Soccer began using yellow and red cards at the 1970 World Cup, from an idea by Ken Aston.
reading: Soccer players come from many countries. They do not all speak the same language. A referee's words can be missed.
Ken Aston was an English referee. He watched a traffic light change from yellow to red. He thought of colored *cards*. Yellow means a warning. Red means the player must leave.
The cards were first used at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico. Now players and fans see the same signal, in any language.

words.d: a colored card a soccer referee holds up to warn a player or send a player off
the soccer championship between national teams

look.title: A Signal Without Words
look.text: Picture a referee in a stadium in Mexico. The player speaks German. The referee speaks English. The fans speak Spanish. The referee holds up one yellow card.
look.prompt: How does a card help when people speak different languages?

check.q: What gave Ken Aston the idea for colored cards?
check.why: Aston thought of the cards while watching a traffic light.

check.q: What does a red card mean?
check.why: A red card means the player must leave the game.

check.q: Where were the cards first used?
check.why: The cards were first used at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico.

lessons.title: A Story About Hand Signs
lessons.mainIdea: People tell a story that a Deaf player, William Hoy, helped umpires use hand signs.
reading: William Hoy played Major League Baseball from 1888 to 1902. He was *Deaf*. He could not hear an umpire call out. He was a fast, smart outfielder.
Many people tell a story about Hoy. They say umpires began raising an arm for a strike so he could see the call. Historians still argue about whether that is how hand signs began.
What we know for sure is this. Umpires today use arm signals. Players and fans can see a call from far away.

words.d: not able to hear, or part of the community of people who cannot hear
a sign that sends a message without words

look.title: Seeing a Call
look.text: Picture a baseball park in 1890. The crowd is loud. The umpire shouts, but the outfielder is far away. Now the umpire raises his right arm high. Everyone in the park can see it.
look.prompt: Who is helped when a call can be seen as well as heard?

check.q: Who was William Hoy?
check.why: William Hoy was a Deaf player in Major League Baseball from 1888 to 1902.

check.q: Do historians agree that Hoy started umpire hand signs?
choices: Yes, it is in the rule book.
No, they still argue about it.
check.why: The Hoy story is well loved, but historians still argue about it.

check.q: Why do hand signals help at a game?
choices: People can see a call from far away.
check.why: Arm signals let players and fans see a call from far away.

lessons.title: How Many on a Side
lessons.mainIdea: Rule books say how many players each team may have in the game at once.
reading: In 1886, soccer groups formed a board. They came from England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland. It is the International Football Association Board. It still keeps the *Laws of the Game*.
Law 3 is about players. Each soccer team may have eleven on the field. Other sports write their own numbers. Basketball has five on a side.

words.d: the written rules of soccer, kept by the International Football Association Board
a group of players who share one side in a game

look.title: Players on Each Side
look.unit: players per team in the game at once
look.cite: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 3; Official Baseball Rules; NHL Official Rules; NFHS Basketball Rules
look.prompt: Which sport has the most players on a side? Which has the fewest?

check.q: How many players may one soccer team have on the field?
check.why: Law 3 of the Laws of the Game allows no more than eleven.

check.q: When was the group that keeps soccer's Laws of the Game formed?
check.why: The International Football Association Board was formed in 1886.

check.q: How many basketball players are on each side?
check.why: Basketball has five players on each side.

lessons.title: Nine, Then Five
lessons.mainIdea: Naismith's first basketball game had nine players on a side; later rules set five.
reading: Naismith's class in 1891 had eighteen students. So the first basketball game had nine players on each team. Everyone in the class got to play.
Other gyms had different numbers of players. A crowded floor made the game rough. By the late 1890s, basketball rules set *five* players on each side.

words.d: a written statement of what players may and may not do

look.title: Naismith's Big Class
look.text: Naismith wrote that his class had eighteen men. He split them into two teams of nine so that everyone could take part in the first game.
look.cite: James Naismith, Basketball: Its Origin and Development (1941)
look.prompt: Why did the first game have nine players on each side?

check.q: How many students were in Naismith's 1891 class?
check.why: Naismith's class had eighteen students, so each team had nine.

check.q: Why did the number of players change?
choices: A crowded floor made the game rough.
check.why: Too many players on one floor made the game rough, so rules set five.

check.q: About when did basketball rules set five players on a side?
check.why: By the late 1890s, basketball rules set five players on each side.

lessons.title: Numbers, Not Names
lessons.mainIdea: In 1929, the New York Yankees gave numbers by batting order, so Babe Ruth wore number 3.
reading: In 1929, the New York Yankees wore *numbers* on their backs all season. Each number matched a player's batting turn.
Babe Ruth was the most famous player in baseball. He batted third, so he wore number 3. Lou Gehrig batted fourth and wore number 4. The number showed a turn, not fame.

words.d: the digits on a uniform that help people tell players apart
the list that sets which baseball player takes a turn at bat first, second and so on

look.title: Reading the Backs
look.text: Picture the Yankees in 1929. Numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 stand in a row. Number 3 is Babe Ruth. Number 4 is Lou Gehrig. The numbers go in the order they came up to bat.
look.prompt: Why did Babe Ruth not get number 1, even though he was so famous?

check.q: Why did Babe Ruth wear number 3 in 1929?
check.why: Yankee numbers matched the batting order, and Ruth batted third.

check.q: Which team gave numbers by batting order in 1929?
check.why: The New York Yankees wore numbers by batting order in 1929.

check.q: What number did Lou Gehrig wear?
check.why: Gehrig batted fourth, so he wore number 4.

choices: the stone starting line at Olympia
review.why: The balbis was the stone starting line in a Greek stadium.

review.q: What happened to the soccer referee in 1891?
choices: He moved onto the field to make the calls.
He was replaced by two umpires.
review.why: In 1891 the referee walked onto the field and made the calls for both teams.

review.q: Who thought of yellow and red cards?
review.why: Ken Aston, an English referee, thought of the cards.

review.q: What does Law 3 of the Laws of the Game set?
choices: how many players a team may have
review.why: Law 3 says each team may have no more than eleven players on the field.

review.q: How many players were on each side in Naismith's first game?
review.why: Naismith split eighteen students into two teams of nine.

review.q: What did a Yankee's number show in 1929?
choices: his place in the batting order
review.why: Yankee numbers in 1929 matched each player's place in the batting order.
